A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable text, mathematics, figures, tables, and appendices. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: Appendix B.3 reports original numerical experiments on a synthetic simplex-domain function, including sampled smoothness relationships and dimensional trends in Figures 1–2.

after.justification: Appendix C.3 retains the synthetic experiments. Section 2.3 and Appendix B additionally report nanoGPT training experiments on FineWeb, with results in Figures 1–2.

M1.justification: Section 5 adds composite mirror descent with a convex regularizer inside the proximal update. Section 4 introduces a horizon-dependent stochastic mirror-descent stepsize schedule alongside the earlier adaptive anytime version, retained in Appendix J. The original deterministic updates largely remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds nanoGPT-124M pretraining on FineWeb, extending actual empirical coverage from synthetic simplex functions to language-model training. The earlier synthetic coverage remains in Appendix C.

E2.justification: The synthetic comparison retains the same Euclidean and non-Euclidean smoothness formulations. unScion supplies the new training trajectory; no additional competing optimizer is evaluated against the paper's methods.

E3.justification: The new nanoGPT study introduces trajectory-based smoothness estimates using successive stochastic gradients and parameter changes, layer-specific norms, affine approximations, and relative-MSE diagnostics. The retained synthetic protocol still uses 500 sampled simplex points and the same dimension sweep.

E4.justification: Figures 1–2 add a real-model case study testing whether generalized smoothness tracks training curvature, including an embedding parameter group and four transformer blocks. This substantially extends the earlier synthetic dimension-sensitivity analysis, retained as Figures 3–4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new plots provide point estimates and fitting errors. Added high-probability convergence guarantees are theoretical results.

E6.justification: New nanoGPT results report relative MSE 0.0020 for the embedding group and 0.0080, 0.0151, 0.0244, and 0.0767 for blocks 0–3. The synthetic fitted trend, 1.87 times n^(-0.43), remains unchanged. These are additional diagnostic results, without a same-setting optimizer performance comparison.

T1.justification: v3 removes the bounded-domain assumption from the deterministic guarantees, replaces D² with initial Bregman distance, and adds a bounded-trajectory argument in Lemma F.3. Theorem 4.2 and Appendix I introduce sub-Gaussian last-iterate analysis; Theorem 5.1 and Appendix K add non-convex composite guarantees. The earlier anytime theorem remains as Theorem J.3.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand from convex mirror descent and anytime stochastic convergence under generalized bounded noise to sharp last-iterate stochastic guarantees and non-convex composite optimization. They also explicitly claim relevance to LLM pretraining and post-training.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the nanoGPT traces as supporting practical generalized smoothness and claims noise-adaptive convergence recovering deterministic rates. It replaces v2's stated incompatibility with sub-Gaussian analysis with a chain-of-events explanation. Appendix J also newly distinguishes bounded generating-function range from uniformly bounded Bregman divergence.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds implementation information identifying PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel, eight NVIDIA 4090 GPUs with 24GB each, and a third-party experimental codebase. Further settings are referred to cited material. The synthetic autograd and linear-programming details remain.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted discussions of recent clipping, sign-based, and zeroth-order optimization research, plus references supporting composite optimization and nanoGPT experiments. The central positioning relative to Li et al. and relative smoothness remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: the full literature review moves to Appendix A, main-text proofs move into algorithm-specific appendices, and the stochastic discussion is rewritten around the new result. The abstract and conclusion are revised accordingly.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Table 1 gains a convexity column and a composite-MD row and displays the new stochastic result. Two nanoGPT figures are added; the earlier synthetic figures remain as Figures 3–4.

improvement.justification: Broader deterministic guarantees and nanoGPT diagnostics add value beyond v2. However, Appendix I states a stepsize inconsistent with Theorem 4.2 and drops a G B(x*,x0)/sqrt(T) term without establishing the claimed noise-free O(1/T) specialization. These unresolved issues affect a central new contribution, leaving the overall balance between added value and theoretical reliability uncertain.
